flashcards.front: What is the primary threat vector for Application Threat Auditing?
flashcards.back_definition: Adversaries exploit undetected file modifications on application directory to bypass standard perimeter security controls.
flashcards.back_example: Example: FIM Alert: Hash mismatch calculated on /usr/local/bin/gateway_agent
flashcards.back_confusion: Don't confuse this threat with other layers (like physical breaches or certificate revocations) which target different assets.
flashcards.back_hook: Recall: undetected file modifications is the unlocked door; application directory is what the attacker wants to steal.

flashcards.front: How does the security team mitigate Application Threat Auditing threats?
flashcards.back_definition: Deploying and enforcing SHA-256 file integrity monitoring directly hardens application directory and blocks unauthorized connections.
flashcards.back_example: Action: Update security configurations to require SHA-256 file integrity monitoring.
flashcards.back_confusion: Don't confuse mitigation (actively blocking the exploit) with detection (simply logging or alerting the event).
flashcards.back_hook: Mitigation is the shield; detection is the security camera.

flashcards.front: How do analysts detect exploitation of Application Threat Auditing?
flashcards.back_definition: By auditing event data and implementing logic flags built to alert on checksum baseline mismatches.
flashcards.back_example: Syslog trace: FIM Alert: Hash mismatch calculated on /usr/local/bin/gateway_agent
flashcards.back_confusion: Don't confuse signature-based detection (matching known strings) with anomaly-based detection (mapping dynamic standard deviations).
flashcards.back_hook: Detection is looking for the fingerprint left behind by the threat.
